ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the circuit diagram there is an operational amplifier. Connected to the non-inverting input terminal at the upper left is an RC frequency-selective positive feedback network composed of a 1 nF capacitor and a 158 kΩ resistor; the inverting input terminal is grounded through a 10 kΩ resistor and obtains negative feedback from the output terminal through a feedback resistor. The network inside the dashed box is composed of a 100 kΩ resistor and two diodes connected in opposite directions, connected in the feedback path from the output terminal to the inverting input terminal, and together with the upper 22.1 kΩ feedback branch affects the feedback at the inverting terminal. Reasoning: Since the dashed-box network is located in the negative feedback/gain control path, and not in the RC frequency-selective network at the non-inverting terminal, it does not determine the oscillation frequency. When oscillation has just begun, the diodes are basically cut off, and the closed-loop gain is relatively high, which is favorable for starting oscillation; when the output amplitude increases, the diodes conduct, causing the feedback equivalent resistance to change, thereby reducing the op-amp closed-loop gain and making it approach the value required to maintain oscillation. This can prevent the op-amp from entering saturation, and limit and stabilize the oscillation amplitude.

method.method_draft: First describe the visible circuit: the op amp has an RC frequency-selective positive-feedback network on the + input and a resistive negative-feedback network on the − input. The dotted network is connected in the output-to-inverting-input feedback path, so it cannot set the oscillation frequency; instead it changes the feedback/gain. Use Barkhausen/gain-control reasoning: as oscillation amplitude grows, the diodes conduct and alter the effective feedback resistance, reducing closed-loop gain toward the value needed for sustained oscillation. Therefore its function is amplitude stabilization, keeping the op amp out of saturation and producing a nearly fixed-amplitude sinusoid.
